newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers, bosses meet to sign deals.
newsitem.headline: French truckers, bosses meet to sign deals.

text.p: Striking French truck drivers met employers on Friday to sign deals on some of their demands and union leaders said they were keen to end the crippling 12-day-old stoppage provided the government stepped in.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe urged a fast solution, cautioning that "the consequences (of a prolonged strike) on our economy, on many companies, on many workers risk being very damaging".
He ruled out using force to clear truckers' blockades at 230 main roads and almost half the country's petrol depots.

As junior transport minister Anne-Marie Idrac pledged a decree within 15 days to define working hours, unions and industry bosses met at the transport ministry two hours later than planned. There was no explanation for the delay.
Union leaders said they were eager to negotiate provided the government guaranteed by decree payment for all hours worked, including unloading time and compulsory rest periods.
"We don't want to prolong the strike artificially," said Claude Debons of the Socialist-led CFDT. "The condition for lifting the roadblocks is a guarantee on working hours."

"We have come to seek a clear reply from the government on working time. If we have to work all day, we'll work all day," said Alain Renault, representative of the second largest union among the truckers, the Communist-led CGT.

Unions and employers were due to sign agreements already reached in talks this week on early retirement at 55 instead of 60 for drivers with 25 years at the wheel, sick pay, travel expenses and a ban on Sunday driving.
But the related issues of pay and hours remained outstanding when talks broke down on Thursday. Full payment for all hours worked would be equivalent to a substantial pay rise.
Truckers say they often work more than 200 hours a month, with many hours unpaid as they wait to load and unload.

"People have said for years that the issue (of working hours) must be settled and we need to go further. We must clarify in an irrefutable manner what working hours should involve, what should be paid for. We need a decree," Idrac said.
But Idrac insisted pay was an issue for unions and bosses and not for the government.
The unions demand pay rises of an average 23 percent. The employers have offered a one percent real pay rise and a 1,500 franc ($300) one-time bonus.
Bosses said that while they could not increase their offer, they would be flexible in re-arranging its terms. Spokesman Rene Petit said raising the pay offer would ruin many haulage firms.
The strike, in the crucial pre-Christmas commercial period, has cost European food and haulage industries tens of millions of dollars a day, prompting protests from France's neighbours.
Truckers have also sealed off France's 13 oil refineries. Petrol rationing has spread and about 8,000 of 18,000 petrol stations were either dry or feeling shortages.

The roadblocks have forced the closures of some factories for lack of supplies and cut deliveries of perishable goods ranging from fish to fruit and flowers. In Rouen, in Normandy, 9,000 workers from various sectors were temporarily laid off.
In London, Britain's Transport Secretary George Young summoned the French ambassador on Thursday to express concern over the stranding of British lorries, officials said.
The blockade has also stranded up to 14,000 Spanish trucks and idled about 90 percent of Portugal's total truck fleet. Belgian ports were clogged by British-bound lorries avoiding France.
